data.text:
I ran one search per claim. Most of what came back was manufacturer, trade and encyclopedia material. I found no primary government or engineering document for claims 0 and 1, so those two verdicts are weaker than the others.

**Claim 0: an average backyard pool holds about 15,000 to 20,000 gallons. Verdict: supported, with a caveat.**
- Vita Filters (a manufacturer) says "The average residential swimming pool holds between 15,000 and 20,000 gallons of water." https://www.vitafilters.com/blogs/news/how-many-gallons-are-in-my-pool
- Swimming Pool Steve calculates an average of 17,280 gallons. That is for a 16'x32' pool with a 4.5' average depth. https://www.swimmingpoolsteve.com/pages/average-pool.html
- A pool-service company gives a wider range. It says a 16x32 ft pool is typical and holds "between 10,000 and 20,000 gallons." https://westernlehighservices.com/what-is-the-average-pool-size-for-your-backyard/
- The caveat is that these are industry estimates, not survey data. The 15,000–20,000 figure sits at the upper-middle of the range. A safer line would be "roughly 10,000 to 20,000 gallons."

**Claim 1: a pool pump should turn over all the water about once every 8 hours. Verdict: supported in a corrected form.**
- Swim University says "A full turnover usually takes 8 to 10 hours." It calls that the minimum run time for your pump. https://www.swimuniversity.com/run-pool-pump/
- Leslie's says "Most pool owners target an 8–10 hour turnover." https://lesliespool.com/blog/how-to-calculate-pool-pump-run-time.html
- California Pools says industry standards recommend "a minimum target turnover rate of 6 hours." It adds that requirements vary by local health code. https://www.californiapools.com/blog/california-pools-blog/pool-maintenance-care/how-long-should-you-run-your-pool-pump-/
- A US patent filing says "A typical-use pool should have a pump and filtration system capable of pumping the entire contents of the pool through the filters every six hours." https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/12017170
- Another patent filing says home timers typically limit pump operation to "between 8 and 12 hours per day." https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11168911
- **Corrected form:** "Residential pools are commonly run for a turnover of about 8 to 10 hours. Public and commercial standards are stricter, around 6 hours, and local codes vary." The single figure of 8 hours is not a universal rule.

**Claim 2: free chlorine should stay at about 1 to 3 ppm. Verdict: supported in a corrected form.**
- Sensorex says "The ideal range for free chlorine in a pool is between 1-3 parts per million (ppm)." https://sensorex.com/understanding-free-chlorine-levels-in-pools/
- iopool also gives 1–3 ppm for ordinary pools. It gives 0.5–1.5 ppm for saltwater pools. https://iopool.com/blogs/pool-advices/pool-chlorine-levels-what-they-should-be-and-why-they-keep-changing
- Sensorex also reports that the CDC's Model Aquatic Health Code sets a minimum of 1 ppm free chlorine in pools. For spas the minimum is 3 ppm, and the maximum is 10 ppm. https://sensorex.com/free-chlorine-vs-total-chlorine/
- Pool Calculator says the Association of Pool and Spa Professionals recommends 2.0–4.0 ppm. https://www.poolcalculator.com/pool-maintenance/what-should-chlorine-levels-be-in-swimming-pools-and-hot-tubs/
- Beltway Pools gives 2–4 ppm for most residential pools. It adds that CDC guidance is at least 2 ppm when cyanuric acid (stabilizer) is in use. https://www.beltwaypools.com/articles/pool-water-chemistry-101/
- **Corrected form:** "The CDC minimum is 1 ppm. Common residential targets run from 1–3 ppm up to 2–4 ppm, and higher if the pool uses stabilizer." The 3 ppm in the CDC figure is the spa minimum, not a pool maximum.

**Claim 3: water absorbs red light, so deep pool water looks blue. Verdict: supported as written, with a minor refinement.**
- Wikipedia's "Ocean color" article says "water preferentially absorbs red light, which means that blue light remains and is reflected back out of the water." https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_color
- Wikipedia's "Color of water" article says hydrogen bonding in liquid water at 20 °C causes red absorption at around 740 nm and 660 nm. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_of_water
- CNN quotes a scientist who says the blue is noticeable in a large volume of water. The deeper the pool, the bluer it looks. The same happens under artificial lighting. https://www.cnn.com/2016/08/12/sport/why-are-swimming-pools-blue
- The refinement is that real pools also look blue because of the light-colored pool surface and sky reflections. The absorption effect is real but weak in a typical 1–3 m pool. "Large volume" matters, as does "deep".
